path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Equilibrium Thermodynamics/01 - Foundations - equilibrium, equations of state and the chemical potential/ET-01 - The criterion for phase equilibrium.md
gap: The transfer calculation does not explicitly explain why each transfer is independent or distinguish stationarity from stability.

edits.old: **Step 4: equilibrium and direction.** At the minimum of $G$, (4) must vanish for any small transfer, so
edits.new:
**Step 4: equilibrium and direction.** At the minimum of $G$, (4) must vanish for any small transfer, so

The important choice in (4) is to transfer just one component while conserving its total amount. Such a transfer can be made in either direction, independently of transfers of the other components. If its coefficient were non-zero, one direction would lower $G$, so the state could not be an equilibrium minimum. This is why each chemical potential must match separately; a cancellation between transfers of different components would not suffice.

Equality removes the immediate driving force, but it is a stationary-state condition. To establish stable equilibrium, the state must also have the lowest accessible $G$. The supercooled-water example illustrates the distinction: the bulk free-energy advantage determines which phase wins, while creating an interface can delay its appearance.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Equilibrium Thermodynamics/01 - Foundations - equilibrium, equations of state and the chemical potential/ET-02 - Equations of state and departure functions.md
gap: The purpose of the Maxwell substitution and the relation of an isothermal derivative to throttling remain compressed.

edits.old: *Reason:* the right side contains only $P$–$\underline{V}$–$T$ quantities, which the EOS provides.
edits.new:
*Reason:* the right side contains only $P$–$\underline{V}$–$T$ quantities, which the EOS provides.

The substitution does more than remove an inconvenient symbol. An EOS measures how the fluid expands when heated at fixed pressure; the Maxwell relation turns that measurable response into the entropy change on compression. Equation (8) combines that entropy contribution with the direct $\underline{V}\,dP$ contribution to enthalpy. Their exact cancellation for an ideal gas explains why its enthalpy depends only on temperature.

For throttling, pressure and temperature change together while enthalpy stays fixed: $0=\underline{C}_P\,dT+(\partial\underline{H}/\partial P)_T\,dP$. With positive $\underline{C}_P$, a negative pressure derivative therefore makes a pressure decrease accompany a temperature decrease. This connects the sign in the departure calculation to cooling without treating the throttle itself as isothermal.

edits.new:
*Reason:* dividing by $n$ gives the molar form. This is Euler's theorem for homogeneous functions. It says the partial molar volumes are the right "shares" of the total: they add up exactly to the mixture volume.

Equation (13) uses all the partial molar volumes at the *final mixture composition*. It does not say that ethanol and water carry fixed parcels of volume from their pure states into the bottle. Adding ethanol changes the surroundings of water as well as those of ethanol; the measured total volume includes that collective rearrangement. The derivative assigns its net effect to the increment being added.

That is why the bottle calculation first finds composition from the amounts in the recipe, then reads both partial molar volumes at that composition, and only then reconstructs the final volume. Using pure volumes in the last step would erase the very change in molecular surroundings that the graph measures.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Equilibrium Thermodynamics/01 - Foundations - equilibrium, equations of state and the chemical potential/ET-04 - Chemical potential and the Gibbs–Duhem equation.md
gap: The cancellation establishing Gibbs–Duhem and its distinction from opposite absolute deviations need a sharper explanation.

edits.old: This is the Gibbs–Duhem equation. Dividing by $n$ gives the mole-fraction form.
edits.new:
This is the Gibbs–Duhem equation. Dividing by $n$ gives the mole-fraction form.

The cancellation has a useful meaning. Changing amounts already contributes $\sum_i\mu_i\,dn_i$ to $dG$ through the fundamental relation. Differentiating $G=\sum_i n_i\mu_i$ appears to add a second contribution because the chemical potentials also change. At fixed $T$ and $P$, that extra weighted contribution must cancel. Gibbs–Duhem prevents the same change in mixture Gibbs energy from being counted twice.

It constrains slopes along a composition change, not the signs of departures from the pure liquids. Both partial molar volumes can therefore be below their pure values in the bottle example, even though their composition derivatives have opposite signs. Recovering one component's curve from the other also needs a reference value, normally the known pure-component endpoint, to fix the integration constant.

gap: The real-minus-ideal subtraction and the role of composition held fixed in the EOS integral need linking.

edits.old: The first two terms are the ideal-gas-mixture value. The integral is the real-fluid correction. It is finite because $\bar V_i - RT/P$ stays bounded as $P\to 0$.
edits.new:
The first two terms are the ideal-gas-mixture value. The integral is the real-fluid correction. It is finite because $\bar V_i - RT/P$ stays bounded as $P\to 0$.

The subtraction is made between two fluids at the same temperature, pressure and composition. It removes only the effect of intermolecular interactions, leaving the entropy of mixing in the ideal reference. Holding composition fixed along the integration path matters: otherwise $\mu_i$ would change because both pressure and the molecular environment were changing, and the pressure integral alone would miss part of that change.

In the bottle example, volume contraction tests the *pressure derivative* of the chemical-potential model. It establishes non-ideality, but it does not determine the whole Gibbs-energy correction at one pressure. A function's slope cannot fix its value without a reference; activity measurements supply the additional information.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Equilibrium Thermodynamics/02 - Fugacity/ET-06 - The Poynting correction (vapour pressure under an inert gas).md
gap: Total liquid pressure and gas partial pressure are distinct, but their contrasting changes in a pressure experiment remain implicit.

edits.old: **Step 4: equate chemical potentials.** At equilibrium $\underline{G}^{l}(T,P) = \mu^{v}(T,P^{\mathrm{VAP}})$. Substitute (29) and (30), then cancel the two reference terms using (28):
edits.new:
**Step 4: equate chemical potentials.** At equilibrium $\underline{G}^{l}(T,P) = \mu^{v}(T,P^{\mathrm{VAP}})$. Substitute (29) and (30), then cancel the two reference terms using (28):

Imagine adding more insoluble gas while keeping temperature fixed and liquid present. The liquid feels the higher *total* pressure, so its chemical potential rises. In the ideal gas mixture, however, water responds to its own *partial* pressure. Equilibrium requires that partial pressure to rise just enough to match the liquid-side increase. The water mole fraction can nevertheless fall, because the total gas pressure is increasing much more strongly.

Thus a higher equilibrium water partial pressure does not mean a larger fraction of water in the gas. The Poynting factor answers the former question. To obtain the fraction, divide the resulting $P^{\mathrm{VAP}}$ by the specified total pressure.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Equilibrium Thermodynamics/02 - Fugacity/ET-07 - Fugacity, definition and meaning.md
gap: Fugacity as an exponential coordinate can be confused with a rate or with absolute pressure.

edits.old: **Direction.** $f^{l} > \bar f_w^{v}$, so water leaves the liquid: it evaporates.
edits.new:
**Direction.** $f^{l} > \bar f_w^{v}$, so water leaves the liquid: it evaporates.

To see why a pressure-like ratio gives the driving force, write (39) for water in each phase and subtract. The identical ideal-gas reference cancels, leaving $\mu^{l}-\mu^{v}=RT\ln(f^{l}/\bar f_w^{v})$. A ratio above unity gives evaporation, a ratio below unity gives condensation, and unity gives no net transfer. The absolute size of either fugacity is less informative than this comparison.

The humidity example therefore establishes the direction and thermodynamic incentive for transfer. It does not give an evaporation rate: that also needs transport through the gas next to the surface and the heat needed to sustain evaporation. Equal fugacities describe the endpoint, not how quickly it is reached.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Equilibrium Thermodynamics/02 - Fugacity/ET-08 - Fugacity from volumetric data and the fugacity coefficient.md

edits.old:
**What $\phi$ measures.** By (49), $\phi$ is the residual Gibbs energy expressed as a factor on pressure. Its sign relative to 1 reflects the accumulated volume departure along the isotherm, not just the volume at the final pressure.
- $\phi < 1$: the integrated volume departure is negative. Attractions often dominate over much of the path, lowering the Gibbs energy and escaping tendency. This is typical of gases at modest pressures below their Boyle temperature, and of vapours.

- $\phi < 1$: the integrated volume departure is negative. Attractions often dominate over much of the path, lowering the Gibbs energy and escaping tendency. This is typical of gases at modest pressures below their Boyle temperature, and of vapours.

One way to read (47) is to build the correction in small pressure increments. Wherever $Z<1$, the next increment lowers $\ln\phi$; wherever $Z>1$, it raises it. The differentiation must act on the *total* excess Gibbs energy, $ng(x_1)$, because adding a mole both increases the system's size and changes its composition. The product rule accounts for the extra amount through $g$; the chain rule accounts for the changed environment through the derivative term. Differentiating $g$ alone would keep only the second effect and would not give a partial molar property.

For Margules, unlike contacts disappear at either pure endpoint, so $g$ vanishes there. Yet inserting one trace molecule into the other pure liquid creates unlike contacts immediately, so the derivative, and hence its infinite-dilution excess chemical potential, can remain finite. Zero mixture excess energy at a pure endpoint does not require zero dilute-solute non-ideality.

The denominator $n$ in $\sum_{i<j}A_{ij}n_in_j/n$ changes when $n_k$ is increased. path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Equilibrium Thermodynamics/03 - Activity coefficients and excess Gibbs energy/ET-13 - Worked example, liquid oxygen–argon.md
gap: The example compares nonideal vapour enrichment with Raoult but can obscure which phase is oxygen-richer.

edits.old: The liquid boils at a 4 % higher pressure than an ideal mixture would. Its vapour is slightly richer in oxygen than Raoult's law predicts, because oxygen, the more dilute component, has the larger $\gamma$.
edits.new:
The liquid boils at a 4 % higher pressure than an ideal mixture would. Its vapour is slightly richer in oxygen than Raoult's law predicts, because oxygen, the more dilute component, has the larger $\gamma$.

There are two different baselines here. The vapour is richer in oxygen than the *Raoult prediction*, because oxygen receives the larger activity-coefficient correction. It is still poorer in oxygen than the liquid itself: the reported $y_1$ is below the specified $x_1$. Argon remains the more volatile component under these conditions.

The reason is that vapour composition depends on both components' partial pressures, not only oxygen's $\gamma_1$. Adding the two contributions first determines the bubble pressure; dividing oxygen's contribution by that total then determines $y_1$. A larger activity coefficient is therefore not, by itself, a ranking of volatility between different substances.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Equilibrium Thermodynamics/04 - Measuring activity coefficients and freezing-point depression/ET-16 - Worked example, ethylene glycol–water freezing and the eutectic.md
gap: Why the higher of two computed freezing temperatures is encountered first, and what remains fixed during freezing, need making explicit.

edits.old: The real mixture freezes at about −45 °C, 8–12 K **lower** than the ideal prediction.
edits.new:
The real mixture freezes at about −45 °C, 8–12 K **lower** than the ideal prediction.

Cooling starts from above both candidate freezing temperatures, so the *higher* branch is encountered first. Once ice appears, it removes water without removing glycol. The overall composition of the closed sample is unchanged, but the remaining liquid becomes glycol-richer and follows the ice branch towards the eutectic. A vertical cooling path for the whole sample is therefore not a constant-composition path for its liquid phase.

Equation (86) finds where one liquid composition can simultaneously satisfy both pure-solid equilibrium conditions. Above that intersection only one solid is stable against the liquid at a time; at the intersection both can coexist. The measured first-freezing point of the water-rich mixture constrains water activity on the ice branch, rather than locating the eutectic of the real system.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Equilibrium Thermodynamics/06 - Phase rule, osmosis, droplets and bubbles/ET-22 - Osmotic equilibrium.md
gap: The pressure normalisation and composition-dependent endpoint need connecting to reverse osmosis.

edits.old: **Step 5: combine with (113).**
edits.new:
**Step 5: combine with (113).**

The pure-solvent reference is written at each side's actual pressure so that the pressure difference appears explicitly before the common reference is cancelled. The two remaining terms oppose one another: mixing lowers the solvent's chemical potential in the solution, and additional pressure raises it. Dividing their balance by the solvent molar volume converts an energy deficit per mole into the pressure required to cancel it.

At this pressure difference the net solvent flux is zero. Raising solution-side pressure further reverses the chemical-potential difference and drives solvent towards the pure side. During real reverse osmosis, removal of solvent concentrates the retained solute, so the opposing osmotic pressure rises. The quoted seawater threshold is therefore an initial equilibrium requirement rather than a single pressure that guarantees the same driving force throughout concentration.

The large pressure in the droplet is not the vapour pressure surrounding it. It acts on a dense liquid, whose chemical potential responds through its small molar volume. The gas matches that energy change through a logarithmic change of its much smaller pressure. This explains how the table can contain a large Laplace pressure alongside only a modest relative vapour-pressure enhancement.

The critical-radius argument holds the surrounding temperature and supersaturation fixed, as if the droplet exchanges molecules with a large vapour reservoir. A slightly smaller droplet then needs a higher vapour pressure than that reservoir provides and shrinks further. In a closed vessel with appreciable condensation, the vapour inventory and supersaturation also change, so that feedback must be included before inferring the fate of the whole droplet population.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Equilibrium Thermodynamics/06 - Phase rule, osmosis, droplets and bubbles/ET-24 - Bubbles, superheating and boiling.md
gap: The different compressed phases in bubbles versus droplets and separate meanings of superheat and boiling elevation need connecting.

edits.old: The liquid must be hot enough that its *flat-surface* vapour pressure equals the pressure inside the bubble.
edits.new:
The liquid must be hot enough that its *flat-surface* vapour pressure equals the pressure inside the bubble.

For a droplet, the compressed phase is liquid and the surrounding vapour changes only slightly. For a bubble, the compressed phase is vapour itself: the gas must supply the entire Laplace pressure. Raising temperature increases its saturation pressure until this mechanical requirement and chemical equilibrium can both hold. As the bubble grows, the required pressure excess falls, making further growth easier.

The salt calculation addresses a separate cause of a higher boiling temperature. Solute changes the bulk liquid's chemical potential even for a flat interface; small-radius superheat arises because forming the curved interface requires extra pressure. A nucleation site can reduce the latter while leaving the solvent-activity effect intact, which explains why the appearance of bubbles on adding salt is not a measure of the equilibrium boiling-point elevation.

**Step 2: what happens at a mixture critical point.** Along a coexistence path towards the critical point, the phase compositions and densities both converge: $\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{y}$ and $\underline{V}^{l}\to\underline{V}^{v}$. The tie line shrinks to zero. For a cubic EOS, the liquid and vapour roots then coalesce. Equal fugacities alone do not locate a critical point, because (146) also has a trivial equal-composition, equal-root solution at every homogeneous state; a critical calculation additionally checks loss of stability.

A single homogeneous fluid always has the same fugacity as an identical copy of itself. That is why assigning both calculation phases the same composition and EOS root solves the equality equations without demonstrating coexistence. A meaningful two-phase calculation must first find distinct states and then test their stability and material balances.

Approaching a genuine critical point from coexistence removes those distinctions continuously: the composition gap and density gap both disappear. An azeotrope removes only the composition gap. This is why a zero-width tie line on a composition plot needs density or stability information before it can be interpreted as criticality.

**Gibbs energy gain.** $\Delta\underline{G}_{\mathrm{mix}}/RT$ is −0.068 for the homogeneous equimolar liquid, and −0.104 at the tangent points. Both reported mixing Gibbs energies are negative relative to the unmixed *pure* liquids. Yet the two partially mixed liquids have the lower value. Mixing spontaneously from pure components therefore does not prove that one homogeneous liquid is the final state: it can be favourable to mix partially and still favourable to separate into two compositions.

The chord represents that alternative while conserving the overall composition. Its endpoints cannot be chosen merely as the nearest minima unless symmetry makes their common tangent horizontal. edits.old: The measured (Fickian) coefficient is therefore
edits.new:
The measured (Fickian) coefficient is therefore

The conversion separates two questions. The mobility coefficient describes how readily molecules respond to a given chemical-potential gradient. The thermodynamic factor describes how much chemical-potential gradient a given composition gradient creates. Diffusion can therefore slow because the restoring force weakens even when molecules remain mobile.

Inside the spinodal the factor changes sign, but the mobility need not become negative: material still moves towards lower chemical potential. It runs uphill in concentration because, there, increasing concentration lowers chemical potential. Using a negative Fickian coefficient alone at arbitrarily short length scales would not describe the developing interface; the omitted gradient free energy supplies the additional physics needed for a spatial phase-separation model.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Equilibrium Thermodynamics/12 - Vapour–liquid–liquid equilibrium and steam distillation/ET-42 - Vapour–liquid–liquid equilibrium.md
gap: Fixed three-phase temperature can seem incompatible with changing composition and phase amounts during boiling.

edits.new:
Any feed between $x_1^{\mathrm{I}}$ and $x_1^{\mathrm{II}}$ starts boiling at the same $T^{*}$, the lowest boiling temperature of the system.

The three-phase line fixes the compositions of the phases, not their amounts. Heat can convert some liquid into vapour while the amounts of the two liquid layers adjust to conserve both components. As long as both layers remain, they supply the same common activities and the same equilibrium vapour, so temperature need not rise.

Once a layer is exhausted, its equilibrium condition no longer constrains the system. There are only two phases, so an intensive freedom reappears at fixed pressure and the boiling temperature can change. The special overall composition equal to the three-phase vapour composition permits both layers to disappear together; otherwise the remaining layer carries the excess of one component into the subsequent two-phase stage.
